steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our tool paper on GiveMeLabeledIssues, a system that recommends open source issues to contributors by labeling them with API domains. Explain why finding suitable issues is hard, what existing issue-labeling work misses, why API-domain labels help, and briefly describe the tool, how it was trained, and how well it performs.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
It is hard for contributors to find issues to work on in Open Source Software (OSS) projects, because it is difficult to tell which skills an issue requires. Labeling the issues manually can help, but manual work means more effort for maintainers, and many projects end up not labeling their issues.

To make issue labeling easier, several studies proposed mining software repositories to tag issues with labels like bug/non-bug and good-first-issue (which helps newcomers find a suitable task). But newcomers to a project have many different skill levels, and these approaches don't say which skills are needed to work on the tasks.

APIs encapsulate modules that have specific functionality. If we can predict which APIs are used to solve an issue, we can guide new contributors on what to contribute. But projects include thousands of different APIs, so adding every API as a label would hurt the user experience. To keep the number of labels manageable, we grouped the APIs into domains for labeling.

- Previous results
  - API domains: "UI," "DB," "Test"; previously 31 domains; label set varies by project
  - Santos et al.: experiment with developers, labels helped find matching tasks; precision 0.755, recall 0.747, F-measure 0.751
- GiveMeLabeledIssues: web tool; API-domain labels for open issues; JabRef, PowerToys, Audacity; select project + skills -> open issues
- Training / evaluation: closed issue title/body + APIs from pull requests; 83.8% precision, 78.5% recall per project

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
It is hard for contributors to find issues to work on in Open Source Software (OSS) projects, because it is difficult to tell which skills an issue requires. Labeling the issues manually can help, but manual work means more effort for maintainers, and many projects end up not labeling their issues.

To make issue labeling easier, several studies proposed mining software repositories to tag issues with labels like bug/non-bug and good-first-issue (which helps newcomers find a suitable task). But newcomers to a project have many different skill levels, and these approaches don't say which skills are needed to work on the tasks.

APIs encapsulate modules that have specific functionality. If we can predict which APIs are used to solve an issue, we can guide new contributors on what to contribute. But projects include thousands of different APIs, so adding every API as a label would hurt the user experience. To keep the number of labels manageable, we grouped the APIs into domains for labeling.

In our study, API domains are categories of APIs, like "UI," "DB," "Test," and so on. In our previous work we used 31 distinct API domains. But the set of possible API-domain labels is different for each project, since each project needs different skills and expertise. In another work, Santos et al. evaluated the API domain labels in an empirical experiment with developers. That study showed that the labels let contributors find OSS tasks matching their expertise more efficiently. The Santos et al. study had promising results for classifying issues by API-Domain, with precision of 0.755, recall of 0.747 and F-measure of 0.751.

Based on this idea we implemented GiveMeLabeledIssues, which classifies issues for potential contributors. GiveMeLabeledIssues is a web tool that gives API-domain labels for the open issues in registered projects. Right now it works with three open-source projects: JabRef, PowerToys, and Audacity. Users can select a project, enter their skill set (using our categories), and get a list of open issues that would need those skills.

We trained the tool on the title and body text of closed issues and the APIs used in the code that solves each issue, which we gathered from pull requests. We evaluated the tool with closed issues as the ground truth, and when training and testing models for individual projects we got an average of 83.8% precision and 78.5% recall.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Contributors struggle to find issues to work on in Open Source Software (OSS) projects because it is difficult to determine the skills required to work on an issue [1]. Labeling issues manually can help [2], but manual work increases maintainers' effort, and many projects end up not labeling their issues [3].

To facilitate issue labeling, several studies have proposed mining software repositories to tag issues with labels such as bug/non-bug and good-first-issue (to help newcomers find a suitable task) [4,5,6,7]. However, newcomers to a project have a variety of skill levels, and these approaches do not indicate the skills needed to work on the tasks.

APIs encapsulate modules with specific functionality. If we can predict the APIs used to solve an issue, we can guide new contributors on what to contribute. However, since projects include thousands of different APIs, adding each API as a label would harm the user experience. To keep the number of labels manageable, we classified the APIs into domains for labeling [8,2].

In our study, API domains represent categories of APIs such as "UI," "DB," "Test," etc. In our previous work, we used 31 distinct API domains [8]. We acknowledge, however, that the set of possible API-domain labels varies by project, as each project requires different skills and expertise. In another work, Santos et al. [9] evaluated the API domain labels in an empirical experiment with developers, which showed that the labels enabled contributors to find OSS tasks matching their expertise more efficiently. The study showed promising results when classifying issues by API-Domain, with precision, recall, and F-measure scores of 0.755, 0.747, and 0.751, respectively.

Following this idea, we implemented GiveMeLabeledIssues to classify issues for potential contributors. GiveMeLabeledIssues is a web tool that indicates API-domain labels for open issues in registered projects. It currently works with three open-source projects: JabRef, PowerToys, and Audacity. The tool lets users select a project, input their skill set (in terms of our categories), and receive a list of open issues that would require those skills.

We trained the tool with the title and body text of closed issues and the APIs used in the code that solves each issue, as gathered from pull requests. Evaluating the tool with closed issues as the ground truth, we found an average of 83.8% precision and 78.5% recall when training and testing models for individual projects.
